Beyond SAEs: Consistent Concept
Discovery with Sparse Coding

Jinho Choi ††thanks: This work was done during a research visit at Helmholtz Munich. Affiliation: KAIST Affiliation: Helmholtz Munich    Hyesu Lim Affiliation: Helmholtz Munich    Jaegul Choo Affiliation: KAIST    Steffen Schneider ††thanks: Correspondence: steffen.schneider@helmholtz-munich.de Affiliation: Helmholtz Munich
Abstract

Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) explain foundation model representations by decomposing activations into sparse combinations of learned dictionary atoms. However, the learned dictionaries can vary across training runs, limiting the reliability and reproducibility of SAE-based analyses. We propose Consistent Sparse Dictionary Learning (ConSDL), which replaces the standard linear encoder with per-sample sparse coding. This is motivated by our synthetic analysis showing that coefficients from a single linear encoder pass are suboptimal compared with those obtained by per-sample optimization, suggesting that sparse coding is a reliable mechanism for dictionary learning. Across 16 synthetic settings, ConSDL achieves near-perfect dictionary and coefficient recovery. These gains translate to state-of-the-art cross-seed consistency across four vision and language settings, where ConSDL improves dictionary and coefficient consistency by 17.6% and 35.9%, respectively, over the average of six SAE baselines.

1 Introduction

Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) (Cunningham et al., 2023) have become a widely used approach for analyzing the internal representations of foundation models. SAEs decompose each model activation into a sparse linear combination of vectors from a learned overcomplete dictionary. Empirically, these dictionary vectors often align with human-interpretable concepts, such as colors, textures, and objects in vision models (Thasarathan et al., 2025) or characters, words, and syntactic patterns in language models (Elhage et al., 2022; Bricken et al., 2023). Importantly, these concepts can be learned without a predefined vocabulary, enabling scalable explanations of model behavior in vision (Lim et al., 2025; Pach et al., 2026) and language (Templeton et al., 2026), audits of hidden biases in models and datasets (Ahsan and Wallace, 2025; Choi et al., 2026), and identification of candidate factors in scientific and medical data (Dasdelen et al., 2025; Nerrise et al., 2026).

Yet, a critical limitation remains before SAEs can serve as practical tools for analysis. SAEs trained on the same data with the same configuration can learn substantially different dictionaries across random seeds (Paulo and Belrose, 2025). This limits reproducibility and reliability. More fundamentally, it raises the question of whether the features learned by SAEs genuinely reflect the model’s internal representations or are artifacts of the training procedure. Recent work has further heightened this concern by showing that SAEs can fail to recover known ground-truth features in controlled synthetic settings (Korznikov et al., 2026; Pacela et al., 2026).

In this paper, we propose Consistent Sparse Dictionary Learning (ConSDL) to make sparse decompositions of model activations consistent across independent training runs, enabling reliable and reproducible analysis. To this end, ConSDL replaces the linear encoder of SAEs with per-sample sparse coding. The algorithm design is motivated by prior work showing that coefficients predicted by a single encoder pass can be suboptimal compared with those obtained by per-sample optimization (O’Neill et al., 2024). We hypothesize that updating the dictionary with these suboptimal coefficients contributes to inconsistency across training runs. ConSDL therefore uses per-sample sparse coding throughout training to obtain coefficients before each dictionary update. To make this procedure stable in practice, we additionally use coefficient refitting to correct shrinkage from the sparsity penalty and a co-active similarity regularizer to reduce dictionary redundancy.

Across diverse synthetic and real-world settings, ConSDL consistently outperforms existing SAEs. In controlled synthetic experiments, ConSDL achieves near-perfect recovery of ground-truth dictionaries and coefficients, even with larger dictionaries and highly imbalanced atom-selection probabilities, where existing methods degrade. These results support our hypothesis that improved coefficient estimation leads to more consistent dictionary learning. ConSDL substantially improves dictionary and coefficient consistency over existing methods on vision and language foundation models.

Our contributions are threefold. First, we introduce ConSDL, which incorporates per-sample sparse coding to produce consistent sparse decompositions across training runs. Second, we systematically study SAE recovery under synthetic conditions and identify when existing methods fail and what factors contribute to these failures. Third, we show that ConSDL improves cross-seed dictionary and coefficient consistency on foundation-model activations across multiple vision and language backbones, dictionary widths, and sparsity levels.

2 Related work

Consistency of SAEs. Recent work has drawn attention to the inconsistency of SAEs, showing that independent training runs can learn substantially different dictionaries (Paulo and Belrose, 2025). Fel et al. (2025) improve dictionary consistency by constraining dictionary atoms to lie within the convex hull of the activation data. Nelson et al. (2026b) instead regularizes the dictionary geometry to reduce ambiguity among sparse codes, improving dictionary and coefficient consistency. However, these studies differ in key experimental choices, including dictionary size, sparsity, and training procedure, making direct comparison difficult. Song et al. (2025) further show that SAE consistency can vary substantially across such configurations. It therefore remains unclear whether the reported gains hold under matched settings. We address this by comparing existing methods across a broad range of settings using the same evaluation protocol.

Sparse coding and dictionary learning. Given a fixed dictionary, sparse coding infers a sparse coefficient to reconstruct each input as a linear combination of dictionary codes (Olshausen and Field, 1997). A common formulation uses an ℓ1\ell_{1} penalty and can be solved with ISTA (Daubechies et al., 2004) or its accelerated variant FISTA (Beck and Teboulle, 2009), while LISTA (Gregor and LeCun, 2010) unrolls ISTA into a fixed-depth network with learned parameters for faster inference. Alternatively, matching pursuit greedily selects atoms that best explain the current residual (Mallat and Zhang, 1993). Dictionary learning jointly learns the dictionary by alternating between sparse coefficient estimation and dictionary updates (Aharon et al., 2006; Mairal et al., 2010). Our proposed ConSDL adopts this alternating formulation, using FISTA for per-sample sparse inference before each dictionary update. Under suitable assumptions, such iterative approaches are theoretically guaranteed to recover the underlying dictionary and coefficients (Agarwal et al., 2016).

From amortized inference to per-sample sparse coding. Standard SAEs use a shared learned encoder to predict sparse coefficients rather than optimizing them separately for each input. This amortized inference (Marino et al., 2018) avoids costly per-sample optimization and enables efficient large-scale training, but at a cost to coefficient quality. O’Neill et al. (2024) show that optimizing coefficients directly under a fixed dictionary substantially improves recovery. Sun et al. (2026) connect amortized inference to feature absorption, splitting, and dead atoms. Joung and Bae (2026) retain an amortized encoder but iteratively refine its predicted coefficients during dictionary learning. Pacela et al. (2026) instead remove the learned encoder and use per-sample sparse coding throughout training, but report degraded recovery for larger dictionaries. Our ConSDL builds on this non-amortized approach while improving its stability and scalability to foundation-model activations.

Recovery guarantees for sparse coding and dictionary learning Sparse recovery theory characterizes when the underlying coefficients can be recovered from observations generated by a known dictionary (Donoho and Elad, 2003; Candes et al., 2006). Exact recovery is possible when coefficients are sufficiently sparse and the dictionary atoms are sufficiently distinct, so that different sparse codes do not produce the same observation (Donoho and Elad, 2003). Restricted isometry provides a stronger formal condition by requiring the dictionary to approximately preserve the geometry of sparse vectors (Candes et al., 2006). When the dictionary is also unknown, the problem additionally requires identifying the dictionary from multiple sparse observations. Under suitable assumptions, including sufficient observations and an initialization close to the ground-truth dictionary, alternating minimization can recover both an overcomplete dictionary and its coefficients (Agarwal et al., 2016). Additional related work is discussed in Appendix A.

3 Method

We propose Consistent Sparse Dictionary Learning (ConSDL) to improve the consistency of dictionaries and coefficients across training runs (Fig. 1). ConSDL replaces the learned encoder with per-input coefficient optimization and updates the dictionary from these estimates. It then refits the magnitudes of the selected coefficients without the sparsity penalty to correct shrinkage from sparse coding, and encourages distinct co-active atoms by penalizing the similarity of the most similar co-active pair.

3.1 Per-sample Sparse Coding

Let 𝐱∈ℝd\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} denote a model activation with dimension dd, which we aim to decompose into a linear combination of mm dictionary atoms weighted by non-negative, sparse coefficient vector. Let Wdec∈ℝd×mW_{\mathrm{dec}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times m} denote the learned dictionary, corresponding to the decoder weight in an SAE. Its jj-th column 𝐰j∈ℝd\mathbf{w}_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} represents a unit-norm dictionary atom. Let 𝐛dec∈ℝd\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{dec}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} denote the decoder bias, and 𝐚∈ℝ≥0m\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{m} denote the nonnegative coefficient vector, with aj∈ℝa_{j}\in\mathbb{R} specifying the contribution of atom jj to the reconstruction.

Standard SAEs use a linear encoder followed by a non-linearity to predict the sparse coefficients 𝐚\mathbf{a} from each input in a single forward pass. These coefficients directly influence the gradients used to update each dictionary atom during training, yet coefficients produced by a single encoder pass can be suboptimal compared with those optimized for the current dictionary (O’Neill et al., 2024). We therefore replace the encoder in a conventional SAE with per-sample sparse coding and infer the coefficients for each input as the solution to the optimization problem:

𝐚sc​(𝐱)=arg​min𝐚≥0⁡12​‖𝐱−Wdec​𝐚−𝐛dec‖22+λ​‖𝐚‖1,\mathbf{a}^{\mathrm{sc}}(\mathbf{x})=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\mathbf{a}\geq 0}\frac{1}{2}\left\|\mathbf{x}-W_{\mathrm{dec}}\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{dec}}\right\|_{2}^{2}+\lambda\|\mathbf{a}\|_{1}, (1)

where λ>0\lambda>0 controls the sparsity penalty. We estimate the solution using the Fast Iterative Shrinkage-Thresholding Algorithm (FISTA; Beck and Teboulle, 2009). Each FISTA iteration updates the coefficients by taking a gradient step on the reconstruction term, followed by nonnegative soft thresholding for the ℓ1\ell_{1} penalty.

3.2 Coefficient Refitting

While the ℓ1\ell_{1} penalty promotes sparsity by penalizing coefficient magnitude, it also introduces shrinkage bias: even after the active atoms are correctly identified, the optimization objective favors smaller nonzero coefficients to reduce the penalty (Zou, 2006). Using these shrunken coefficients directly for decoder updates can underestimate the contributions of the selected atoms (Tolooshams and Ba, 2021). We therefore retain the nonzero coefficients identified by FISTA and refit them without the ℓ1\ell_{1} penalty, following post-selection refitting procedures in sparse estimation (Figueiredo et al., 2007; Chzhen et al., 2019). Collecting the indices of non-zero coefficients in the support Ssc​(𝐱)={j:ajsc​(𝐱)>0}S^{\mathrm{sc}}(\mathbf{x})=\{j:a_{j}^{\mathrm{sc}}(\mathbf{x})>0\}, we solve

𝐚refit​(𝐱)=arg​minaj​∀j∈Ssc​(𝐱)⁡12​‖𝐱−Wdec​𝐚−𝐛dec‖22,\mathbf{a}^{\mathrm{refit}}(\mathbf{x})=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\begin{subarray}{c}a_{j}\forall j\in S^{\mathrm{sc}}(\mathbf{x})\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{2}\left\|\mathbf{x}-W_{\mathrm{dec}}\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{dec}}\right\|_{2}^{2}, (2)

using projected gradient descent initialized from 𝐚sc​(𝐱)\mathbf{a}^{\mathrm{sc}}(\mathbf{x}), constraining the coefficients to remain nonnegative and supported on Ssc​(𝐱)S^{\mathrm{sc}}(\mathbf{x}). Thus, refitting adjusts only the magnitudes of the selected coefficients without activating new atoms. Additional details on the FISTA optimization and refitting procedure are provided in Appendix B.

3.3 Co-active Similarity Regularization

Per-sample sparse coding improves coefficient estimation, but applying it throughout dictionary learning can still lead multiple atoms to converge to similar directions, resulting in redundant dictionary elements. To stabilize dictionary learning in practice, we introduce a co-active similarity regularizer that penalizes high similarity only between atoms active for the same sample, rather than between all atom pairs in the dictionary.

For each input 𝐱i\mathbf{x}_{i}, let Ai={𝐰j:ai,jrefit>0}A_{i}=\{\mathbf{w}_{j}:a_{i,j}^{\mathrm{refit}}>0\} denote the set of active dictionary atoms, where jj refers to the atom index. For each 𝐰j∈Ai\mathbf{w}_{j}\in A_{i}, we define its most similar co-active atom as

𝐰~i,j=arg​max𝐰∈Ai∖{𝐰j}⁡𝐰j⊤​𝐰,si,j=𝐰j⊤​𝐰~i,j.\widetilde{\mathbf{w}}_{i,j}=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\mathbf{w}\in A_{i}\setminus\{\mathbf{w}_{j}\}}\mathbf{w}_{j}^{\top}\mathbf{w},\qquad s_{i,j}=\mathbf{w}_{j}^{\top}\widetilde{\mathbf{w}}_{i,j}. (3)

where si,js_{i,j} is their cosine similarity, since the atoms are unit normalized. To focus the regularization on highly similar pairs, we follow margin-based contrastive objectives (Hadsell et al., 2006) and formulate the co-active similarity penalty as

ℒsim=1|𝒱μ|​∑(i,j)∈𝒱μ(si,j−μ)2,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sim}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}_{\mu}|}\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{V}_{\mu}}\left(s_{i,j}-\mu\right)^{2}, (4)

where μ∈[0,1)\mu\in[0,1) is a similarity margin and 𝒱μ={(i,j):𝐰j∈Ai,si,j>μ}\mathcal{V}_{\mu}=\{(i,j):\mathbf{w}_{j}\in A_{i},\ s_{i,j}>\mu\} is the set of matched co-active pairs whose similarity exceeds the margin. Implementation details of the regularizer are provided in Appendix B.

3.4 Training Objective and Alternating Optimization

Given the refitted coefficients, we define the reconstruction loss as

ℒrec=12​‖𝐱−Wdec​𝐚refit​(𝐱)−𝐛dec‖22.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}=\frac{1}{2}\left\|\mathbf{x}-W_{\mathrm{dec}}\mathbf{a}^{\mathrm{refit}}(\mathbf{x})-\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{dec}}\right\|_{2}^{2}. (5)

The overall training objective is ℒ=ℒrec+γsim​ℒsim,\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}+\gamma_{\mathrm{sim}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sim}}, where γsim>0\gamma_{\mathrm{sim}}>0 controls the strength of co-active similarity regularization. For each update, we first infer and refit the coefficients under the current dictionary and identify the co-active atom pairs. These quantities are then held fixed while optimizing WdecW_{\mathrm{dec}} and 𝐛dec\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{dec}}. Thus, gradients do not propagate through coefficient estimation or pair selection, and training alternates between per-sample sparse coding and dictionary updates. Full optimization details are provided in Appendix B, with hyperparameter settings in Appendix D.

4 Synthetic Analysis of Dictionary and Coefficient Recovery

To study the conditions under which existing SAE methods recover the underlying dictionary and coefficients, and whether ConSDL improves recovery where they fail, we use controlled synthetic data with a known ground-truth decomposition.

4.1 Experimental Setup

Synthetic data generation. We generate synthetic data as 𝐱=∑i=1mai​𝐰i,\mathbf{x}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}a_{i}\mathbf{w}_{i}, where 𝐱∈ℝd\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is an observed activation, 𝐰i∈ℝd\mathbf{w}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} denotes a ground-truth dictionary atom, and ai∈ℝ≥0a_{i}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} is its nonnegative coefficient. In the baseline setting, we use activation dimension d=768d=768, dictionary width m=3072m=3072, and an expected k=60 active atoms per sample (Fig. 2A). Following prior synthetic SAE studies (Korznikov et al., 2026; O’Neill et al., 2024), we sample dictionary atoms independently from an isotropic Gaussian distribution and normalize them to unit norm. For each sample, atoms are selected independently with equal probability, yielding random sparse supports over an approximately incoherent dictionary, as commonly assumed in sparse coding analyses (Arora et al., 2015). Each nonzero coefficient is drawn from a log-normal distribution with expected value 11.

We extend the baseline setting along two axes motivated by properties of foundation-model representations: dictionary size and atom-selection imbalance. First, we vary the ground-truth dictionary width over 4×4\times, 8×8\times, 12×12\times, and 16×16\times the activation dimension, corresponding to m=3072m=3072–1228812288. This range reflects evidence that larger dictionaries continue to uncover additional concepts in foundation model activations (Templeton et al., 2026). Second, we vary atom-selection imbalance using Zipf exponents β∈{0,0.5,0.7,1.0}\beta\in\{0,0.5,0.7,1.0\}, where β=0\beta=0 corresponds to uniform selection and larger values produce increasingly long-tailed frequencies, reflecting the highly imbalanced concept frequencies in web-scale pretraining data (Udandarao et al., 2024). This results in 16 synthetic configurations.

Baselines. We compare a standard ReLU SAE (Cunningham et al., 2023) with TopK (Gao et al., 2025), BatchTopK (Bussmann et al., 2024), Matryoshka SAE (Bussmann et al., 2025), MP-SAE (Costa et al., 2026), and iSAE (Hindupur et al., 2026). For each synthetic configuration, we generate 10610^{6} observations and train each method for five epochs, reducing the likelihood that recovery failures arise from insufficient data or training. We repeat each experiment with three random seeds.

Metrics. We evaluate dictionary recovery using decoder cosine similarity (DCS) (Paulo and Belrose, 2025) after Hungarian matching to the ground-truth dictionary. Coefficient recovery is measured by mean coefficient correlation (MCC) (Pacela et al., 2026) under the same matching. For cross-seed consistency, we apply the same metrics between independently trained runs and average over all seed pairs. Higher values indicate better recovery or consistency. Full metric definitions and experimental details are provided in Appendix D.

4.2 Findings

Recovery strongly depends on the data setting. Despite differences across SAE variants, dictionary and coefficient recovery are generally high for smaller dictionaries and less long-tailed atom selection distributions (lower-left region of each heatmap in Fig. 2B). As dictionary size grows and atom selection becomes more long-tailed, both decline sharply (upper-right region). This sensitivity may help explain why prior synthetic studies have reported both successful (Song et al., 2025) and failed (Pacela et al., 2026) SAE recovery. Since it is unclear which setting best reflects real model activations, these results motivate methods that remain reliable across a wider range of conditions.

Amortization gap in coefficient inference. Even in settings with high dictionary recovery, the encoder does not fully recover the corresponding coefficients. One possible explanation is the amortization gap identified in prior work (O’Neill et al., 2024). We examine this by re-optimizing the coefficients for each sample while keeping the learned dictionary fixed. This improves both coefficient recovery and input reconstruction (Table 1 and 7), showing that the encoder leaves recoverable error in coefficient inference. However, when dictionary recovery is poor, coefficient re-optimization yields limited gains, suggesting that a more fundamental solution requires reliable dictionary learning.

ConSDL remains robust under challenging synthetic conditions. Across all 16 synthetic settings, ConSDL achieves near-perfect recovery of both the ground-truth coefficients and dictionary, including conditions where existing SAE methods degrade (Fig. 2B). This shows that incorporating per-sample sparse coding into dictionary learning not only addresses the coefficient-inference gap, but also improves dictionary recovery when incorporated into dictionary learning. By recovering nearly the same ground-truth decomposition across runs, ConSDL also achieves high cross-seed consistency. Full results are provided in Appendix E (Tables 11–14).

Cross-seed consistency is associated with ground-truth recovery. Across the synthetic sweeps, higher cross-seed consistency corresponds to stronger ground-truth recovery (Fig. 2C). Decoder consistency is strongly correlated with dictionary recovery (Pearson r=0.90r=0.90, Spearman ρ=0.88\rho=0.88), while coefficient consistency shows an even stronger correlation with coefficient recovery (r=0.99r=0.99, ρ=0.98\rho=0.98). Although cross-seed consistency does not by itself establish ground-truth recovery, these strong correlations support its use as a complementary measure for real model activations, where the ground truth is unavailable.

5 Evaluation on Foundation Model Activations

We next evaluate whether the gains observed in synthetic settings extend to foundation-model activations in vision and language domains. Since ground-truth decompositions are unavailable, we use cross-seed consistency as the primary evaluation criterion.

5.1 Experimental Setup and Evaluation

Foundation model activations. For vision, we train SAEs on penultimate-layer activations from CLIP ViT-B/16 (Radford et al., 2021) and DINOv2 (Oquab et al., 2023). We use ImageNet (Russakovsky et al., 2015) and include both class-token and spatial-token activations following prior work (Lim et al., 2025), training each SAE for one epoch over approximately 1.2M images. For language, we train SAEs on layer-9 activations from GPT-2 Small (Radford et al., 2019) and Pythia-160M (Biderman et al., 2023). We train each SAE on 500M FineWeb tokens (Penedo et al., 2024) with a context length of 1024. The activation dimension is 768 for all four models. We evaluate the trained SAEs on the ImageNet validation set for vision and on 20M FineWeb tokens for language. Additional model, data, and training details are provided in Appendix D.4.

Baselines and metrics. We use the same SAE baselines as in the synthetic evaluation. We evaluate dictionary widths of 4×4\times, 8×8\times, and 16×16\times the activation dimension, each at three sparsity levels, ℓ0≈32\ell_{0}\approx 32, 6464, and 128128. Because ground-truth decompositions are unavailable for foundation models, we evaluate cross-seed consistency of the dictionary and coefficients by training each configuration with three random seeds and computing DCS and MCC between independently trained runs, as in the synthetic evaluation. We further report dictionary utilization metrics to assess whether improved consistency comes at the cost of dictionary capacity. We measure the usable atom fraction, defined as the fraction of atoms that are neither dead nor duplicated. Dead atoms are never activated, while duplicated atoms point in highly similar decoder directions, reducing concept diversity.

5.2 Main Results

ConSDL is more consistent than baselines across vision and language backbones. Across 36 configurations spanning four backbones, three dictionary sizes, and three sparsity levels, ConSDL improves both dictionary and coefficient consistency over existing SAE baselines (Fig. 3). Averaged across backbones, ConSDL achieves a DCS of 0.84 and an MCC of 0.78, corresponding to relative gains of 17.6% and 35.9% over the baseline average (Table 8). Compared with the strongest baseline for each metric, ConSDL improves dictionary and coefficient consistency by 1.9% and 13.3% on average. No single baseline is competitive on both metrics: MP-SAE achieves comparable DCS but substantially lower MCC, while ReLU and TopK achieve stronger coefficient consistency among the baselines but lower DCS. ConSDL maintains high consistency in both the learned dictionaries and coefficients across vision and language backbones.11 1 We also compare DCS and MCC under activation-footprint matching instead of decoder cosine similarity, and obtain the same ranking across methods. See Table 6. Detailed results for each backbone and configuration, along with hyperparameter sensitivity analyses are provided in Appendix E (Tables 15–18 and Fig. 17).

Consistency gains do not come at the cost of dictionary quality. Duplicate atoms appear across several baselines, particularly ReLU and MP-SAE, while TopK-based methods and iSAE contain many dead atoms in some settings. As shown in the dictionary utilization panel of Fig. 3, ConSDL maintains high usable atom fractions across backbones, dictionary sizes, and sparsity levels. Averaged across backbones, ConSDL achieves a usable atom fraction of 1.00, a 5.6% improvement over the baseline average and matching the strongest baseline (Table 8). Reconstruction quality remains at a similar level to the baselines across configurations. We also report input R2R^{2} in Tables 15– 18.

Most ConSDL atoms exhibit high cross-seed consistency. Aggregate dictionary consistency scores do not reveal how consistency is distributed across individual atoms. We therefore examine atom-level consistency, defined as the mean decoder cosine similarity between each anchor atom and its matches in the other two seeds. Most ConSDL atoms exhibit high consistency on CLIP ViT-B/16 and Pythia-160M, whereas many baseline atoms have low consistency, particularly in vision (Fig. 4A). Similar trends are observed for DINOv2-B/14 and GPT-2 Small (Fig. 9). Representative examples show that consistent ConSDL atoms retain similar semantic activation patterns across seeds, whereas selected inconsistent TopK atoms respond to unrelated images or tokens (Fig. 4B). We also examine the number of atoms with consistency above 0.7 across dictionary sizes and sparsity levels (Fig. 10). As dictionary size increases, ConSDL learns more such atoms, while most baselines show slower growth or saturation, particularly in vision. Higher sparsity levels yield smaller gains.

5.3 Sparse Probing Evaluation

Evaluating concept localization with sparse probing. We next use sparse probing (Gurnee et al., 2023) to test whether class relevant information can be captured by a small number of dictionary atoms. Concentrating such information in a few atoms can make the learned representation easier to inspect and interpret. We evaluate vision models on six image classification datasets and language models on 113 binary tasks from SAE-Probes (Kantamneni et al., 2025), using the top one or five most discriminative latents. Additional experimental details are provided in Appendix E.3.

ConSDL preserves sparse probing performance. Across vision and language models, ConSDL performs close to the strongest SAE baselines, achieving the best results in several settings and otherwise differing only marginally (Table 2). This suggests that the improved cross-seed consistency of ConSDL do not come at the cost of information localized to a small number of dictionary atoms. Full results are in Tables 9 and 10.

5.4 Ablation Study

Setup. We ablate coefficient refitting and co-active similarity regularization to identify how each component contributes to the cross-seed consistency of ConSDL. We evaluate 16×16\times dictionaries at ℓ0≈128\ell_{0}\approx 128 on CLIP ViT-B/16 and Pythia-160M (Table 3). Because removing either component changes the resulting sparsity, we tune the sparsity penalty separately for each variant to obtain comparable ℓ0\ell_{0}.

Coefficient refitting stabilizes dictionary learning. Comparing sparse coding (SC) with + Refitting, SC requires a larger λ\lambda to reach a similar sparsity level, especially on Pythia (3.03.0 vs. 1.51.5). This stronger sparsity penalty is accompanied by 9,767 dead atoms and substantially lower reconstruction quality (R2=0.69R^{2}=0.69). This severe failure of SC on Pythia is consistent with prior reports that sparse-coding-based dictionary learning can degrade at larger scales (Pacela et al., 2026). On CLIP, SC does not produce dead atoms but still requires a stronger sparsity penalty. Refitting removes the dead atoms on Pythia and raises R2R^{2} to 0.920.92 on both backbones, from 0.690.69 on Pythia and 0.870.87 on CLIP.

Similarity regularization reduces redundancy. However, + Refitting still leaves thousands of duplicated atoms on both backbones. Comparing + Refitting with Full ConSDL, similarity regularization reduces duplicated atoms from 5,564 to 1 on CLIP and from 3,191 to 0 on Pythia. Although + Refitting achieves higher DCS, its DCS decreases after deduplication across cosine similarity thresholds, whereas Full ConSDL maintains high DCS with almost no duplicates (Fig. 16). The same effect appears without refitting. Applying similarity regularization without refitting (+ Similarity Reg.) also substantially reduces duplication, but does not resolve the instability observed on Pythia. These results indicate that both components are necessary for stable dictionary learning.

6 Analyzing Latent Consistency and Concept Discovery

We further investigate the learned atoms by examining the granularity of their semantic concepts and how these concepts change with dictionary size. We then assess whether cross-seed consistency extends beyond individual atoms to the overall dictionary structure.

6.1 Finer-Grained Concept Discovery

ConSDL captures finer-grained concepts than baseline SAEs. On CLIP ViT-B/16 at 16×16\times expansion (ℓ0≈128\ell_{0}\approx 128), ConSDL learns approximately 9K consistent atoms (cross-seed cosine similarity >0.7>0.7), compared with 4K for ReLU SAE (Fig. 10). To understand what these additional atoms represent, we examine ConSDL atoms with decoder directions similar to a single ReLU atom. In the “beer bottle” example, a ReLU atom broadly responds to beer-related objects, whereas matched ConSDL atoms capture more specific features, such as bottle necks, bubbles, and beer in glasses (Fig. 5). These atoms can activate on the same images while responding to different visual features or regions. A similar pattern appears in Pythia-160M, where a ReLU atom associated with “baseball” matches several ConSDL atoms responding to more specific concepts, including team names, pitching, and field positions, with limited token-level activation overlap (Fig. 11). Across all four backbones, atoms from several baselines more often have multiple ConSDL counterparts than the reverse, extending this pattern beyond individual examples (Figs. 13 and 14).

Larger ConSDL dictionaries reveal more detailed concepts. We next examine how learned concepts change across dictionary sizes. In the “Golden Retriever” example, ConSDL learns several related atoms at 16×16\times that capture different visual attributes, whereas ReLU and TopK largely preserve the original broad concept (Fig. 6). Although the ConSDL atoms share a common association with retrievers, their decoder directions and activation patterns exhibit meaningful differences. A similar pattern appears in Pythia-160M, where a 4×4\times ConSDL atom associated with plants matches several 16×16\times atoms capturing plant species, cultivation, and flowers, while ReLU retains a highly similar plant-related atom across dictionary sizes (Fig. 12). Across all four backbones, consistent ConSDL atoms at 4×4\times are more likely to have multiple counterparts at 16×16\times than those from ReLU or TopK (Fig. 15).

6.2 Cross-Seed Consistency of Dictionary Structure

Measuring cross-seed agreement in cluster sizes and centroids. We next examine whether atom-level consistency extends to the overall structure of the dictionary. We focus on CLIP ViT-B/16 and cluster atoms based on decoder direction similarity. We select one training run as a reference and evaluate whether other runs recover similar cluster sizes and centroids. For cluster sizes, we assign atoms from each run to the nearest reference centroid and compare the resulting cluster sizes using Spearman correlation. For cluster centroids, we independently cluster each run, match its centroids one-to-one to the reference centroids, and measure their cosine similarity. We compare this agreement with that obtained by rerunning kk-means on the reference dictionary to account for clustering variability.

ConSDL preserves fine-grained dictionary structure across seeds. As shown in Fig. 7, ConSDL reproduces both cluster sizes and cluster centroids more consistently across training runs. At 16×16\times expansion and ℓ0≈128\ell_{0}\approx 128, its cluster-size rank correlation reaches 0.950.95, compared with 0.220.22 for Matryoshka (Fig. 7B). ConSDL also achieves the highest normalized centroid agreement at every granularity, with scores of 11, 0.960.96, 0.940.94, and 0.880.88 at 192, 48, 12, and 3 atoms per cluster, respectively (Fig. 7C). A score of 1 indicates that cross-run agreement matches that obtained by rerunning kk-means on the same dictionary. The gap between methods widens at finer granularities, indicating that ConSDL more reliably preserves fine-grained dictionary structure across training runs.

7 Discussion and Limitations

Although ConSDL improves cross-seed consistency over existing SAEs on foundation-model activations, it remains lower than the recovery achieved in synthetic settings. This gap may reflect the greater complexity of real activations, including a larger number of underlying concepts, stronger frequency imbalance, and deviations from the assumption that activations are sparse linear combinations of concept directions. Recent work has also questioned whether all concepts can be represented by individual linear directions, suggesting that some may instead exhibit nonlinear or manifold-like structure (Bhalla et al., 2026). However, some meaningful structure may still be representable by linear directions (Park et al., 2023). ConSDL therefore focuses on improving cross-seed consistency within this sparse linear assumption, rather than addressing whether all concepts can be represented linearly.

ConSDL replaces a single encoder pass with iterative per-sample sparse coding, increasing training cost relative to standard SAE baselines. We analyze training and inference costs in Appendix 5. This additional computation reflects a trade-off between efficiency and improved consistency. Future work could reduce this overhead through more efficient sparse solvers. Furthermore, our experiments focus on relatively small foundation models because evaluating multiple methods across dictionary widths, sparsity, and random seeds is computationally demanding. We therefore do not establish whether the gains in cross-seed consistency extend to models with billions of parameters or substantially larger dictionaries. Evaluating ConSDL at larger scales remains an important direction for future work.

8 Conclusion

In this work, we introduce ConSDL, which revisits classical sparse coding to improve the cross-seed consistency over existing SAEs. By replacing the linear encoder with per-sample sparse coding and incorporating coefficient refitting and regularization against redundancy, ConSDL learns more consistent dictionaries and coefficients. It achieves substantially better ground-truth recovery across diverse synthetic settings. These benefits also transfer to foundation-model activations, where ConSDL improves cross-seed dictionary and coefficient consistency across multiple vision and language backbones, dictionary widths, and sparsity levels, while improving dictionary utilization. Future work will investigate scaling ConSDL to larger foundation models and extending it beyond linear feature representations.

AI use statement

In this work, we used generative AI tools to assist with research ideation and experimental design, implementation of methods and experimental pipelines, retrieval and discovery of related work, drafting portions of the manuscript, and editing for English grammar and clarity. We did not use generative AI tools for other tasks requiring disclosure, and the remaining required-disclosure tasks were not applicable to this work. All AI-assisted research decisions, code, retrieved references, and manuscript text were reviewed, validated, and revised by the authors as appropriate. We take responsibility for the final content of this work, including text, claims, and artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI.

Ethics statement

This work investigates the consistency of sparse representations learned from pretrained foundation models. It does not involve human subjects, personal data collection, or deployment in safety-critical settings. We are not aware of any ethical concerns specific to the proposed method beyond those associated with foundation-model interpretability research.

Reproducibility statement

We provide detailed descriptions of the proposed method, experimental setup, evaluation protocols, and training hyperparameters in the main text and appendix. All datasets and pretrained foundation model checkpoints used in our experiments are publicly available and cited in the corresponding sections. We release our source code and experiment configurations at GitHub, along with trained model weights at Hugging Face.

Appendix

Appendix A Extended Related Work

Improving SAE architectures and dictionaries. SAEs gained growing attention in mechanistic interpretability as their application to large language model activations demonstrated the potential to uncover large numbers of interpretable concepts (Bricken et al., 2023). Subsequent work initially focused on improving reconstruction while maintaining sparse activations. JumpReLU SAEs (Rajamanoharan et al., 2024) use learned activation thresholds to optimize sparsity more directly, while TopK SAEs (Gao et al., 2025) and BatchTopK SAEs (Bussmann et al., 2024) enforce sparsity through explicit feature selection. More recent work has shifted attention beyond reconstruction toward the quality and stability of the learned dictionary. SAEBench evaluates feature-level pathologies such as splitting and absorption (Karvonen et al., 2025), while Matryoshka SAEs explicitly target these failures through nested dictionaries (Bussmann et al., 2025). MP-SAE (Costa et al., 2026) instead predicts coefficients iteratively to better capture correlated concepts that may be missed by a single encoder pass.

Ground-Truth Recovery in Synthetic Settings. The inconsistency of SAE dictionaries raises a more fundamental question of identifiability (Nelson et al., 2026a), namely whether SAEs recover the true underlying decomposition. This cannot be determined from real model activations because the ground truth is unavailable. Prior work has therefore used synthetic data with known dictionaries and sparse coefficients to measure recovery directly, and report substantial recovery failures. (Korznikov et al., 2026; O’Neill et al., 2024; Pacela et al., 2026). However, as with prior consistency studies, the reported results are based on specific data distributions and training settings. It therefore remains unclear when SAE recovery succeeds and when it breaks down. We address this through a broader synthetic study spanning a range of difficulty levels.

Appendix B Implementation Details of ConSDL

We provide additional implementation details for the sparse coding, coefficient refitting, and co-active repulsion procedures described in Sections 3.1 and 3.3.

FISTA optimization. Let 𝐫=𝐱−𝐛dec\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{dec}}. We use the standard FISTA iterations (Beck and Teboulle, 2009), initialized with 𝐚0=𝐚−1=𝟎\mathbf{a}_{0}=\mathbf{a}_{-1}=\mathbf{0} and t0=1t_{0}=1. The momentum update is

tk+1=1+1+4​tk22,𝐲k=𝐚k+tk−1tk+1​(𝐚k−𝐚k−1).t_{k+1}=\frac{1+\sqrt{1+4t_{k}^{2}}}{2},\qquad\mathbf{y}_{k}=\mathbf{a}_{k}+\frac{t_{k}-1}{t_{k+1}}(\mathbf{a}_{k}-\mathbf{a}_{k-1}).

The proximal-gradient update is then

𝐮k=𝐲k−η​Wdec⊤​(Wdec​𝐲k−𝐫),𝐚k+1=[𝐮k−η​λ]+,\mathbf{u}_{k}=\mathbf{y}_{k}-\eta W_{\mathrm{dec}}^{\top}\left(W_{\mathrm{dec}}\mathbf{y}_{k}-\mathbf{r}\right),\qquad\mathbf{a}_{k+1}=[\mathbf{u}_{k}-\eta\lambda]_{+},

where 𝐫=𝐱−𝐛dec\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{dec}}, λ\lambda controls the sparsity of the inferred coefficients, and [⋅]+[\cdot]_{+} denotes element-wise projection onto nonnegative values.

The step size is set to

η=1σmax​(Wdec)2,\eta=\frac{1}{\sigma_{\max}(W_{\mathrm{dec}})^{2}},

where σmax​(Wdec)\sigma_{\max}(W_{\mathrm{dec}}) is estimated from the current decoder using 32 power iterations. Since the decoder changes during training, the step size is recomputed under the current dictionary.

Coefficient refitting. Let 𝐚sc​(𝐱)\mathbf{a}^{\mathrm{sc}}(\mathbf{x}) denote the coefficient vector returned by the FISTA solve above. Using its selected support Ssc​(𝐱)S^{\mathrm{sc}}(\mathbf{x}) defined in Section 3.1, we initialize 𝐚(0)=𝐚sc​(𝐱)\mathbf{a}^{(0)}=\mathbf{a}^{\mathrm{sc}}(\mathbf{x}) and perform projected gradient descent on the reconstruction objective without the ℓ1\ell_{1} penalty. Each iteration computes

𝐚~(q+1)=𝐚(q)−η​Wdec⊤​(Wdec​𝐚(q)−𝐫),\widetilde{\mathbf{a}}^{(q+1)}=\mathbf{a}^{(q)}-\eta W_{\mathrm{dec}}^{\top}\left(W_{\mathrm{dec}}\mathbf{a}^{(q)}-\mathbf{r}\right),

followed by

aj(q+1)={max⁡(a~j(q+1),0),j∈Ssc​(𝐱),0,j∉Ssc​(𝐱).a_{j}^{(q+1)}=\begin{cases}\max(\widetilde{a}_{j}^{(q+1)},0),&j\in S^{\mathrm{sc}}(\mathbf{x}),\\ 0,&j\notin S^{\mathrm{sc}}(\mathbf{x}).\end{cases}

We use the same step size η\eta as in the FISTA solve and perform 5–30 refitting iterations depending on the experimental setting. In implementation, a numerical threshold of 10−810^{-8} is used to determine the support returned by FISTA.

Co-active similarity loss. Section 3.3 presents the regularizer as a squared margin penalty for clarity. In implementation, we normalize the similarity above the margin and apply a logarithmic transformation. For each matched co-active pair with si,j>μs_{i,j}>\mu, we use

ϕμ​(si,j)=−log⁡[1−11+δ​(si,j−μ1−μ)2],\phi_{\mu}(s_{i,j})=-\log\left[1-\frac{1}{1+\delta}\left(\frac{s_{i,j}-\mu}{1-\mu}\right)^{2}\right],

where δ>0\delta>0 is a small constant that keeps the loss finite as si,j→1s_{i,j}\rightarrow 1. We then compute

ℒsim=1|𝒱μ|​∑(i,j)∈𝒱μϕμ​(si,j),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sim}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}_{\mu}|}\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{V}_{\mu}}\phi_{\mu}(s_{i,j}),

where 𝒱μ={(i,j):𝐰j∈Ai,si,j>μ}\mathcal{V}_{\mu}=\{(i,j):\mathbf{w}_{j}\in A_{i},\ s_{i,j}>\mu\}. The normalization maps similarities between the margin μ\mu and the maximum similarity of 11 to a common range, while the logarithmic transformation increases the penalty as two atoms approach identical directions. When 𝒱μ\mathcal{V}_{\mu} is empty, the similarity loss is set to zero.

Co-active neighbor search. The nearest-neighbor search in Section 3.3 is restricted to the rr most similar decoder atoms for computational efficiency. At every training step, we compute the candidate neighbors from the current normalized decoder using cosine similarity and retain the top r=32r=32 neighbors of each atom, excluding the atom itself. For each input and active atom, we keep only candidates that are also active for that input and select the candidate with the highest cosine similarity. If none of the candidate neighbors is co-active, that atom does not contribute to the repulsion loss.

Full algorithm. Fig. 8 provides Python code summarizing the complete training step and how the components described above are combined. The code also includes renormalization after each dictionary update to maintain the unit-norm constraint on the dictionary atoms throughout training.

Appendix C Computational Cost Analysis

Measurement setup. To compare the computational cost of ConSDL with existing SAE architectures, we measure per-token inference cost, complete training-step cost, and a component-wise breakdown of the training step. Measurements are performed on an NVIDIA H100 80GB GPU using PyTorch 2.2.2 with CUDA 12.1, reporting the median of 20 timed iterations after 5 warm-up iterations. We use matched sparsity budgets of ℓ0=32\ell_{0}=32, 6464, and 128128 for 4×4\times, 8×8\times, and 16×16\times expansion, respectively. Each step processes 4,096 activation tokens for Pythia-160M and 25,216 activation tokens for CLIP ViT-B/16, corresponding to 128 images with 197 tokens each. All costs are normalized per token, and the frozen backbone forward pass is excluded because it is identical across SAE methods.

Inference and training cost. Table 4 compares the per-token test-time inference and training costs of ConSDL with existing SAE architectures across dictionary expansion factors. Because ConSDL performs sparse coding separately for each sample, it requires more computation than conventional SAEs that obtain sparse coefficients with a single encoder pass. MP-SAE also performs iterative computation during both training and inference. In our measurements, we use 10 matching-pursuit iterations during MP-SAE training, while at test time we continue the iterative selection until the target sparsity is reached. Since each MP-SAE iteration selects a latent based on the current residual, its test-time cost increases with sparsity and exceeds that of ConSDL at higher sparsity levels. ConSDL uses a fixed budget of T=30T=30 FISTA iterations and Trefit=5T_{\mathrm{refit}}=5 refitting iterations across all expansion factors. Although ConSDL has higher training cost than MP-SAE and single-pass SAE variants, this additional computation represents a trade-off for substantially higher cross-seed consistency and better dictionary utilization.

Compute cost breakdown. Table 5 breaks down the training cost of ConSDL into sparse coding, coefficient refitting, similarity regularization, and the remaining update. Sparse coding accounts for most of the computation, averaging approximately 69% of the training step across settings. In contrast, coefficient refitting contributes only about 16% on average, despite its substantial effect on consistency observed in the ablation study. Similarity regularization accounts for a smaller fraction of the overall cost, while the remaining decoding and optimization steps contribute only a few percent. The relative cost of each component also remains similar as the dictionary expansion increases, indicating that the additional computation of ConSDL is dominated by the fixed iterative sparse-coding procedure rather than by refitting or similarity regularization.

Appendix D Experimental Details

This section provides experimental details, including baselines (Section D.1) and evaluation metrics (Section D.2) shared across all experiments, followed by details of the synthetic settings (Section D.3) and foundation model experiments (Section D.4).

D.1 Baselines

Standard and sparsity-controlled SAEs. ReLU SAE (Cunningham et al., 2023) produces nonnegative coefficients using a ReLU encoder and an ℓ1\ell_{1} sparsity penalty. TopK SAE (Gao et al., 2025) removes the ℓ1\ell_{1} penalty and retains the kk largest encoder coefficients for each input. BatchTopK SAE (Bussmann et al., 2024) performs this selection jointly across a minibatch, constraining the average number of active coefficients while allowing sparsity to vary across individual inputs. Matryoshka SAE (Bussmann et al., 2025) trains a single ordered dictionary by applying reconstruction objectives to multiple nested prefixes, so that shorter prefixes are also optimized to reconstruct the input rather than relying on the full dictionary (Bussmann et al., 2025). TopK, BatchTopK, and Matryoshka use the AuxK loss (Gao et al., 2025), which provides learning signal to inactive latents by using them to explain the residual reconstruction error. We use an auxiliary-loss coefficient of 1/321/32 and set kaux=din/2k_{\mathrm{aux}}=d_{\mathrm{in}}/2.

Iterative sparse encoding. MP-SAE (Costa et al., 2026) replaces single-pass coefficient inference with an iterative matching-pursuit procedure that repeatedly selects dictionary atoms based on the current reconstruction residual. We include MP-SAE as an alternative approach to iterative sparse coefficient inference.

Consistency-focused SAE. iSAE (Nelson et al., 2026b) modifies TopK using two components designed to improve dictionary and coefficient identifiability. First, it adopts AbsTopK (Zhu et al., 2026), which selects coefficients by magnitude while preserving their signs. This allows a single dictionary atom to contribute with either sign rather than requiring separate atoms for opposite signed contributions. Second, iSAE regularizes the decoder toward an approximate restricted-isometry property (Candes and Tao, 2005; Nelson et al., 2026b), discouraging distinct sparse coefficient vectors from producing nearly identical reconstructions. We use an aRIP regularization weight of 0.10.1

Related baselines excluded from quantitative comparison. We also considered two closely related methods but exclude them from the quantitative comparisons because we could not obtain stable operating points under our experimental settings. Archetypal SAE (Fel et al., 2025) is designed to improve cross-run dictionary consistency by first summarizing the activation distribution with K-means centroids and then learning dictionary atoms from these anchors. DL-FISTA (Pacela et al., 2026) removes the amortized encoder and uses alternating optimization. The original study reports a severe loss of dictionary recovery as the latent dimension increases. We attempted to reproduce both methods across our evaluation settings but were unable to obtain sufficiently stable results for reliable comparison, and therefore omit them from the reported quantitative results.

D.2 Evaluation metrics

We evaluate ConSDL and SAE baselines in terms of input reconstruction, dictionary utilization, and cross-seed consistency.

D.2.1 Reconstruction

A useful sparse representation should retain enough information to reconstruct the original activation. We measure reconstruction quality using input R2R^{2},

R2=1−∑n=1N‖𝐱n−𝐱^n‖22∑n=1N‖𝐱n−𝐱¯‖22,R^{2}=1-\frac{\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left\|\mathbf{x}_{n}-\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{n}\right\|_{2}^{2}}{\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left\|\mathbf{x}_{n}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}\right\|_{2}^{2}},

where 𝐱n\mathbf{x}_{n} and 𝐱^n\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{n} denote the original and reconstructed activations, respectively, and 𝐱¯\bar{\mathbf{x}} denotes the mean activation.

D.2.2 Dictionary utilization

Dead atoms. These represent dictionary capacity that is effectively unused. For atom jj, we define its activation frequency as

pj=1N∑n=1N𝕀[an​j≠0].p_{j}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\mathbb{I}\left[a_{nj}\neq 0\right].

We classify an atom as dead when pj<10−6p_{j}<10^{-6} and report the number of dead atoms.

Duplicated atoms. These represent redundant dictionary capacity, with multiple atoms pointing in nearly identical decoder directions. Prior work measures duplication using pairwise decoder cosine similarity at a single threshold (Mudide et al., 2025), making the result sensitive to the particular threshold and without explicitly identifying groups of mutually similar atoms. We instead exclude dead atoms and apply complete-linkage clustering to the remaining normalized decoder atoms over cosine-similarity thresholds τ∈{0.6,0.7,0.8,0.9}\tau\in\{0.6,0.7,0.8,0.9\}. Complete linkage ensures that every pair of atoms within a duplicate cluster satisfies the similarity criterion. At each threshold, we classify all atoms in clusters of size greater than one as duplicated and report the duplicated-atom count averaged across thresholds.

Usable atom fraction. We summarize dictionary utilization as the fraction of atoms that are neither dead nor duplicated. Let NdeadN_{\mathrm{dead}} denote the number of dead atoms and N¯dup\bar{N}_{\mathrm{dup}} the duplicated-atom count averaged across the thresholds above. We define

Usable​Atom​Fraction=1−Ndead+N¯dupm.\mathrm{Usable\ Atom\ Fraction}=1-\frac{N_{\mathrm{dead}}+\bar{N}_{\mathrm{dup}}}{m}.

Higher values indicate that more of the dictionary capacity is both active and non-redundant.

D.2.3 cross-seed consistency

Decoder consistency. We measure cross seed decoder consistency using one-to-one Hungarian matching between normalized decoder atoms based on cosine similarity, following prior work (Paulo and Belrose, 2025). We refer to the resulting score as decoder cosine similarity (DCS). For each seed pair, DCS is the mean cosine similarity of the matched atoms,

DCSr,s=1m​∑j=1mcos⁡(𝐝j(r),𝐝π⁡(j)(s)),\operatorname{DCS}_{r,s}=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\operatorname{cos}\left(\mathbf{d}_{j}^{(r)},\mathbf{d}_{\pi(j)}^{(s)}\right),

where π\pi denotes the optimal Hungarian assignment. We report DCS averaged over all seed pairs.

Coefficient consistency. We use the same decoder-based assignment to evaluate whether matched atoms exhibit similar coefficient patterns across inputs. For each matched atom pair, we compute the Pearson correlation coefficient between their coefficients across evaluation samples. We report the mean coefficient correlation (MCC), averaged over all matched atom pairs and then over all seed pairs. For computational efficiency, coefficient correlations are computed on a fixed subset of sampled tokens rather than the full evaluation set.

D.2.4 Matching basis

The cross-seed ranking is consistent under both geometric and activation-based matching. Throughout the paper we align dictionaries across seeds with a Hungarian assignment on decoder cosine similarity (πdec\pi_{\mathrm{dec}}). To verify that our conclusions are not an artifact of this geometric choice, we construct a second, independent assignment from activation footprints: for each latent we record its mean activation magnitude on every image of the ImageNet validation split (50K images, 985K tokens), yielding a footprint in ℝ50​K\mathbb{R}^{50\mathrm{K}}, and match seeds by footprint cosine similarity (πfp\pi_{\mathrm{fp}}). We then score three consistency metrics (DCS, MCC, and footprint cosine similarity) on CLIP ViT-B/16 (16×16\times, ℓ0≈128\ell_{0}\approx 128, 3 seeds) under both assignments. Table 6 shows that the two assignments induce the identical ranking for every metric, and Ours ranks first in all six columns. Since πdec\pi_{\mathrm{dec}} requires no forward passes over the dataset, we adopt it as the default matching basis in the main text.

D.3 Details of Synthetic experimental

This section provides additional details for Section 4.

Support and coefficient distributions. We write each ground-truth coefficient as ai=bi​cia_{i}=b_{i}c_{i}, where bi∈0,1b_{i}\in{0,1} determines whether feature ii is active and ci>0c_{i}>0 its activation magnitude. In the default setting, supports are sampled independently as bi∼Bernoulli⁡(pi)b_{i}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p_{i}) with pi=k/mp_{i}=k/m. Consequently, the number of active features varies across observations, with expected sparsity k=60k=60. Conditional on activation, coefficient magnitudes are sampled independently from LogNormal⁡(μ=0,σ=0.25)\mathrm{LogNormal}(\mu=0,\sigma=0.25).

Long-tailed firing probabilities. To vary atom-frequency imbalance independently of the ground-truth dictionary, we randomly permute the atom indices, assign each atom a rank ri∈1,…,mr_{i}\in{1,\ldots,m}, and set pi=min⁡(1,C​ri−β)p_{i}=\min(1,Cr_{i}^{-\beta}), where CC normalizes the expected number of active atoms to k=60k=60 before clipping. We use the four Zipf exponents specified in the main text. Supports are otherwise sampled independently, so this sweep changes marginal atom selection frequencies without introducing explicit co-occurrence correlations.

Training details. We train each SAE for five epochs over a fixed pool of 10610^{6} observations per configuration. Each configuration is trained with three random seeds, {0,1,2}\{0,1,2\}. Unless otherwise stated, all models use a batch size of 128, a learning rate of 10−410^{-4}, and 500 warmup steps followed by a constant learning-rate schedule. For TopK, BatchTopK, Matryoshka, and iSAE, we sweep k∈{60,90,120}k\in\{60,90,120\} and report the best-performing setting for each synthetic configuration. MP-SAE uses 60 matching-pursuit iterations during both training and inference. For ReLU SAE and ConSDL, the sparsity-controlling coefficient is selected separately for each synthetic configuration to obtain comparable sparsity levels. Exact sparsity parameters and experiment-specific hyperparameters are reported in Table 20.

D.4 Details of Foundation Model Experiments

We provide additional details on model backbones and SAE training data (Section D.4.1), training settings (Section D.4.2), and sparse probing protocols (Section E.3).

D.4.1 Model and Data Details

Vision models. For CLIP, we use openai/clip-vit-base-patch16 (https://huggingface.co/openai/clip-vit-base-patch16). Its ViT-B/16 vision encoder has approximately 86M parameters, 12 Transformer blocks, a hidden dimension of 768, 12 attention heads, and a patch size of 16×1616\times 16 for 224×224224\times 224 inputs. For DINOv2, we use facebook/dinov2-base (https://huggingface.co/facebook/dinov2-base), which is a ViT-B/14 model with approximately 86M parameters, 12 Transformer blocks, a hidden dimension of 768, 12 attention heads, and a patch size of 14×1414\times 14.

Vision dataset. For the vision data, we use evanarlian/imagenet_1k_resized_256 (https://huggingface.co/datasets/evanarlian/imagenet_1k_resized_256). This release preserves the original ImageNet-1K splits while resizing the shorter side of each image to 256 pixels. Its training split contains 1,281,167 images and validation split contains 50,000 images

Language models. We use the pretrained Pythia-160M checkpoint EleutherAI/pythia-160m (https://huggingface.co/EleutherAI/pythia-160m). Pythia-160M contains 162M parameters and 12 Transformer layers, with a hidden dimension of 768 and 12 attention heads. For GPT-2 Small, we use openai-community/gpt2 (https://huggingface.co/openai-community/gpt2). GPT-2 Small contains 124M parameters and 12 Transformer layers, with a hidden dimension of 768, 12 attention heads, and a maximum context length of 1024.

Language dataset. We use FineWeb (HuggingFaceFW/fineweb; https://huggingface.co/datasets/HuggingFaceFW/fineweb), a CommonCrawl-based corpus containing more than 18.5T tokens. For each language backbone, we tokenize and cache a fixed subset of 500M tokens using the corresponding model tokenizer. The same token set is reused across random seeds, with only the sequence order shuffled between runs.

D.4.2 Optimization and hyperparameters

Training details. Unless otherwise stated, vision and language experiments use the same optimization settings. We use a learning rate of 3×10−43\times 10^{-4} with 500 linear warmup steps, followed by a constant learning-rate schedule. We train all models with three random seeds, {0,1,2}\{0,1,2\}, where the seed controls both parameter initialization and data ordering. Vision models use batches of 128 images, whereas language models use 4,096 tokens per optimization step.

Architecture-specific settings. For TopK, BatchTopK, Matryoshka, and iSAE, kk is selected according to the target sparsity. MP-SAE uses 10 or 32 matching-pursuit iterations during training. At inference time, matching pursuit is continued until the target L0L_{0} is reached. For ReLU SAE and ConSDL, sparsity is controlled indirectly through the ℓ1\ell_{1} coefficient and sparse-coding penalty, respectively. We therefore consider operating points within ±15%\pm 15\% of the target L0L_{0} and select the setting with the highest DCS ×\times usable atom fraction within this range. Exact sparsity parameters and experiment-specific hyperparameters are reported in Table 19.

Appendix E Full Experimental Results

This section provides full results for the synthetic experiments from Section 4 in Section E.1, and for the foundation model experiments from Section 5 in Section E.2.

E.1 Synthetic Results

Frozen dictionary coefficient re-optimization. To separate coefficient-inference error from dictionary-recovery error, we re-optimize coefficients while keeping each trained decoder fixed (Table 7). For each sample, we replace the amortized encoder output with coefficients obtained by running 50 FISTA iterations against the same learned dictionary, without updating the decoder. We then recompute coefficient recovery (MCC) and input reconstruction R2R^{2}. When the learned dictionary remains accurate, per-sample re-optimization substantially improves MCC and generally improves reconstruction, showing that the amortized encoder can leave recoverable coefficient information unused. As dictionary recovery degrades with larger dictionaries and more long-tailed atom selection frequencies, these gains become much smaller. Better coefficient inference alone therefore cannot compensate for an inaccurate dictionary, motivating improvements to the dictionary learning process itself.

Full results of synthetic experiments. As a supplement to Fig. 2, we report the full synthetic results across all baselines, including input reconstruction, dictionary utilization (# Dead and # Dup.), ground-truth recovery, and cross-seed consistency, in Tables 11, 12, 13, and 14. Existing baselines generally show degraded ground-truth recovery and cross-seed consistency as the settings become more challenging, often accompanied by poorer dictionary utilization. In contrast, our method remains substantially more robust across the sweep, including the largest dictionaries and most strongly long-tailed activation distributions.

E.2 Results on Foundation Model Activations

Atom-level consistency distributions. We present consistency distributions for CLIP ViT-B/16 and Pythia-160M in Fig. 4A, with additional results for DINOv2-B/14 and GPT-2 Small in Fig. 9. Across all four backbones, ConSDL exhibits a greater concentration of high-consistency atoms than most baselines, particularly in vision models. This is also reflected in the number of atoms with consistency above 0.7 across dictionary sizes and sparsity levels (Fig. 10).

Examples of finer-grained concepts in Pythia-160M. We observe similar patterns in Pythia-160M, extending our findings from CLIP ViT-B/16 (Figs. 5 and 6). In the comparison between ConSDL and ReLU SAE (Fig. 11), a ReLU atom broadly responds to baseball-related text, whereas matched ConSDL atoms capture more specific information, including player and team names and gameplay descriptions. In the 4×4\times versus 16×16\times comparison (Fig. 12), a ConSDL atom at 4×4\times matches several 16×16\times atoms associated with plant species, cultivation, and flowers, whereas ReLU retains highly similar plant-related atoms across dictionary sizes. For qualitative interpretation, we examine highly activating tokens and their surrounding contexts from the FineWeb evaluation corpus. We use Claude Opus 5.5 to assign descriptive concept labels based on these examples, relying on the surrounding context when peak activations occur on function words.

One-to-many correspondence across methods. To examine whether the finer-grained concepts observed in examples (Fig. 5 and Fig. 11) reflect a broader pattern across vision and language models, we analyze one-to-many atom correspondence across methods (Fig. 13). Across all four backbones, a greater fraction of consistent ReLU atoms have multiple ConSDL counterparts than vice versa. Averaged across source methods, ConSDL achieves the highest or joint-highest correspondence fraction across all four backbones. This asymmetry persists when requiring three, five, or eight counterparts, and similar trends are observed against TopK (Fig. 14). Together with its low dictionary redundancy, these results suggest that ConSDL often represents features captured by a single baseline atom using multiple, potentially more specific atoms.

One-to-many correspondence across dictionary sizes. While the preceding analysis compares different methods, we now examine atom correspondence between 4×4\times and 16×16\times dictionaries within each method (Fig. 15), extending the qualitative observations in Fig. 6 and Fig. 12. Across the four backbones, 45–55% of consistent ConSDL atoms at 4×4\times have at least two consistent counterparts at 16×16\times, compared with 12–37% for ReLU and substantially lower fractions for TopK. This difference is particularly pronounced in vision, where ConSDL also exhibits higher correspondence fractions when requiring three or five counterparts. Given the low dictionary redundancy of ConSDL, these results support our qualitative observations that larger dictionaries capture multiple distinct but related features associated with broader concepts.

Dictionary consistency and redundancy. In the ablation study (Table 3, removing similarity regularization yields higher DCS but also substantially more duplicate atoms. To examine how these duplicates affect measured consistency, we recompute DCS after deduplication across cosine similarity thresholds from 0.6 to 0.9 (Fig. 16). Without regularization, deduplication at a threshold of 0.6 removes 41% and 29% of atoms in CLIP ViT-B/16 and Pythia-160M, reducing DCS from 0.85 to 0.78 and from 0.84 to 0.79, respectively. As the threshold increases, fewer atoms are removed and DCS approaches its original value. In contrast, ConSDL has no identified duplicate atoms across the tested thresholds while maintaining high DCS. These findings suggest that duplicate atoms can inflate DCS, highlighting the importance of evaluating cross-seed consistency alongside dictionary redundancy. We therefore also report the usable atom fraction, which accounts for both dead and duplicate atoms, throughout our evaluation.

Hyperparameter sensitivity. To assess whether the consistency gains depend on a particular hyperparameter choice, we vary the sparsity penalty λ\lambda and the number of refitting iterations TrefitT_{\mathrm{refit}}, while keeping the FISTA iterations and similarity regularization strength fixed (Fig. 17). Multiple configurations within the target sparsity range outperform the strongest baseline in both DCS and MCC while maintaining nearly full dictionary utilization. Although reconstruction quality varies across configurations and does not consistently exceed the best baseline, the improvements in dictionary and coefficient consistency are not limited to the selected configuration.

Full results on foundation-model activations. We report complete results across three dictionary expansion factors (4×4\times, 8×8\times, and 16×16\times) and three matched sparsity levels (ℓ0≈32\ell_{0}\approx 32, 6464, and 128128). For each configuration, we evaluate reconstruction quality (R2R^{2}), cross-seed dictionary consistency (DCS), coefficient consistency (MCC), and usable atom fraction. Detailed results are provided in Tables 15, 16, 17, and 18 for CLIP ViT-B/16, DINOv2 ViT-B/14, GPT-2 Small, and Pythia-160M, respectively. Table 8 provides a summary.

E.3 Sparse Probing Evaluation

We provide the full sparse probing protocol and results for vision and language models. Following prior work (Gurnee et al., 2023; Karvonen et al., 2025), we identify dictionary atoms that best distinguish positive from negative examples and evaluate probes restricted to the Top-1 or Top-5 selected atoms.

Atom selection. We follow the class-conditional activation criterion used in sparse probing (Gurnee et al., 2023). We first normalize each atom by its mean nonzero activation magnitude and then rank atoms by the absolute difference between their mean normalized activations on positive and negative training examples. Atom selection is performed using only the training split.

Probe construction. We evaluate the Top-1 and Top-5 selected atoms. For Top-1, we use the absolute activation of the selected atom directly as the prediction score, without fitting an additional classifier. For Top-5, we fit a logistic regression classifier using the raw activations of the five selected atoms on the training split and evaluate its decision scores on the evaluation split.

Language benchmarks. For language models, we use the SAE-Probes benchmark (Kantamneni et al., 2025), which consists of 113 binary classification tasks spanning a diverse range of linguistic and semantic concepts. For each task, examples are labeled as positive or negative according to the target concept, and the learned SAE activations are used as probe inputs. We follow the benchmark protocol for constructing the training and evaluation sets and report the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC).

Vision benchmarks. For vision models, following the evaluation strategy of ConceptScope (Choi et al., 2026), we evaluate sparse probing across datasets covering diverse types of visual concepts. We use ImageNet (Russakovsky et al., 2015) with 1,000 object classes, SUN397 (Xiao et al., 2010) with 397 scene categories, Food-101 (Bossard et al., 2014)with 101 food categories, Caltech-256 (Griffin et al., 2007) with 256 object categories, DTD (Cimpoi et al., 2014) with 47 texture categories, and RAF-DB (Li et al., 2017) with 7 facial emotion categories. Each category is treated as a one-vs-rest binary prediction task. We use 50 training images per category for atom selection, and evaluate on the full validation or test split. All available negative examples are used for evaluation. We report the area under the precision–recall curve (AUPRC) because the resulting one-vs-rest tasks are highly imbalanced.

E.4 Analysis: Region carve and cross-seed latent matching

This section examines whether independently trained SAEs decompose the same input in the same way, and whether individual latents recover the same selectivity across seeds.

Region-level decomposition. Figure 18A and Fig. 19A test whether different seeds decompose the same input similarly. We cluster patches or tokens based on their coefficient vectors. At each position, coefficients below 1%1\% of the maximum are discarded and the remainder renormalized. We compare positions using half the L1L_{1} distance between these vectors, ranging from 00 for identical coefficients to 11 for no overlap. Average-linkage hierarchical clustering is then applied separately for each seed to form k=10k=10 regions. Regions are colored by their mean position in the image or text, and agreement across seeds is measured by the adjusted Rand index (ARI).

Organization of matched latents across seeds. Figures 18B–C and 19B–C examine whether latents matched across seeds occupy similar regions of their learned dictionaries and exhibit similar activation behavior. We match latents by decoder cosine similarity and visualize the three dictionaries side by side in a shared UMAP space, fitted on one seed and used to project the other two. We also compare the regions where matched latents activate on the same input and their top-activating samples.

Vision. We analyze CLIP ViT-B/16 at 16×16\times expansion and ℓ0≈128\ell_{0}\approx 128 using an ImageNet validation image. In Fig. 18A, the three seeds produce nearly identical region decompositions, with pairwise ARI values of {0.98,0.98,0.97}\{0.98,0.98,0.97\}, consistently separating the handler, fence and background, and the animals. Panels B and C examine two matched latents active on a patch on the animal’s head. The first responds to animals in close physical contact, such as nuzzling, grooming, and huddling, with activation concentrated around the contact region rather than a particular species. Its top-activating images show the same relation across unrelated classes. The second captures a heart or romance-related pattern and is similarly reproduced across seeds. These examples show that a single patch can be decomposed into distinct latents that recur across independent runs.

Language. We analyze Pythia-160M at 16×16\times expansion and ℓ0≈128\ell_{0}\approx 128 using an example from the 20M-token FineWeb evaluation set. In Fig. 19A, the three seeds produce broadly similar region decompositions, with pairwise ARI values of {0.83,0.65,0.74}\{0.83,0.65,0.74\}. We exclude position 0 because its unusually large activation would otherwise form a separate region. Panels B and C examine two matched latents. The first responds to animal nouns such as tiger, lion, pig, rat, and bear across unrelated contexts and has high decoder similarity across seeds (cos=0.97\cos=0.97 to both). The second responds to sentence-final punctuation and the preceding token. Despite lower decoder similarity (cos=0.65\cos=0.65 and 0.790.79), its top-activating contexts show the same pattern across all three seeds. This suggests that similar activation behavior can persist even when decoder similarity is moderate.
